overview.body:
**Fáfnir** (*fafnir*) ​— Dwarf turned ‌Dragon · ‌figure in Germanic ​heroic legend — ​belongs to the ​Norse tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under the ‌domain "Dwarf turned ​Dragon". The name ​means "figure ‌in Germanic heroic ​legend"[^1].

In the ‌norse tradition, **Fáfnir** ​governed gold, ‌greed, and the ​metamorphosis that greed ​performs. The son ​of Hreiðmarr who ​became the ​dragon of Gnitaheiðr, ‌he is the ​living proof of ‌the curse ​he served: the ‌weregild gold of ​the dwarf Andvari ‌unmade a farmer's ​son into ‌a poison-breathing serpent, ​and turned a ​name that means ‌*the embracer* ‌into an emblem ‌of everything that ​hoarding destroys.

His ​domain is ‌the moral underside ​of heroic legend: ​patricide for an ‌inheritance, kinship dissolved ​by a ​ring, and the ‌slow alchemical change ​of a man ‌into the ​monster that guards ​what he cannot ​use. When Sigurðr's ​sword found his ‌heart, the ‌gold passed on ​— and the ‌curse passed with ​it, through ​the hall of ‌the Gjúkungs to ‌the ruin of ‌the whole ‌Vǫlsung line.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the name ‌as **Fáfnir** and ​serves its temple ​at [fáfnir.com](https://xn--ffnir-xqa.com). ​The restoration preserves ‌at least one ​distinctive feature — ​a diacritic ​or a distinctive ‌letter — that ​the ASCII form ​loses, and exactly ​one historically ‌valid Unicode restoration ​exists, which places ‌the name in ​Tier 1. ‌The plain ASCII ​form *fafnir* survives ‌as a modern ‌convenience imposed ​by the early ​domain-name system; the ​restoration, not the ​fallback, is the ‌form the ‌project defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Younger ​Futhark as ​**ᚠᛅᚠᚾᛁᚱ**. Etymologically ​it means ​"figure ​in Germanic ‌heroic legend"[^1].

​The ​ASCII form ‌*fafnir* survives ​only ‌because the ​early domain-name ‌system ​could not ​carry diacritics; ​it is ​a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ​ancient ‌spelling. The ​Unicode restoration ‌**Fáfnir** ​recovers the ‌stress accent ​of ‌the original ​directly in ​the address ‌bar. ‌The restoration ‌preserves at ​least ​one distinctive ‌feature — ​a ​diacritic or ‌a distinctive ​letter ​— that ‌the ASCII ​form loses, ‌and ​exactly one ​historically valid ​Unicode ​restoration exists, ‌which places ‌the ​name in ‌Tier 1.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

- ‌**f** → ‌**F** ‌— Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**a** ​→ **á** ​— Stress ​on ‌a
- ​**f** → ​**f** ​— Same
‌- **n** ​→ **n** ​— ​Same
- ‌**i** → ​**i** ‌— Same
​- **r** ‌→ ​**r** — ‌Same

The ‌project ​holds the ​domain **fáfnir.com** ​(xn--ffnir-xqa.com) as ​the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sources.citation: Vǫlsunga saga, tr. Morris & Magnússon (Project Gutenberg #1152).
Poetic Edda: Reginsmál, tr. Bellows (Internet Sacred Text Archive).

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed ​pronunciation of ‌the name is ‌**/ˈfɑːv.nir/** — Old ​Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme by phoneme:

​- **á** — ​Long open ​back vowel [ɑː]; ‌the acute marks ​both stress ​and length, like ‌a held 'ah' ​in 'father'
‌- **fn** — ​The fricative is ‌voiced between ​vowels and before ​n, so ​the -fn- cluster ​is realized as ​[vn], not ‌the hard [f] ​of 'fox'
- ‌**r** — ​Final alveolar trill ‌[r], the nominative ​ending of ‌the strong masculine ​noun

For the ‌modern speaker, ​the closest approximation ​is: 'FAHV-neer' — ‌hold the ‌first vowel long ‌like 'ah', ​let the f ​soften to a ‌'v' before ​the n, and ​trill the final ‌r.

Kindred ​and historical forms ​of the name:

‌- **Modern ​Icelandic** — Fáfnir, ‌unchanged in form ​and inflection ​from the medieval ​language
- **Continental ​German** — ‌Fafner, the form ‌Wagner made famous ​in the ‌Ring cycle
- ​**Anglicized** — ​Fafnir, the name ‌stripped of its ‌acute accent

‌Fáfnir is Tier ‌1: the acute ​on á ‌marks stress and ​length on the ​first syllable ​— a feature ‌the ASCII form ​Fafnir loses. ​The form is ​attested throughout the ‌Codex Regius ​poems (Reginsmál, Fáfnismál) ​and in ​Vǫlsunga saga; Cleasby-Vigfusson ‌(s.v. Fáfnir) and ​Zoëga's Concise ‌Dictionary of Old ​Icelandic record the ‌name and ​connect it with ‌the notion of ‌'the embracer' ​(cf. faðmr, 'embrace'). ​The medial -fn- ​was pronounced ​with a voiced ‌fricative, [vn] — ‌hence the ​approximation 'FAHV-neer'.

sources.citation: Vǫlsunga saga, tr. Morris & Magnússon (Project Gutenberg #1152).

original-script.body:
The ​name is ‌preserved in ‌Younger Futhark ​as **ᚠᛅᚠᚾᛁᚱ**.[^1]

​The scholarly ​transliteration is ​*fafnir*.

The ​rendering proceeds ‌step by ​step:

- ​ᚠ (fé) ‌writes both ​/f/ and ‌/v/
- ​ᛅ (ár) ‌writes /a/, ​/á/ and ​/æ/
- ​ᚾ (nauðr) ​writes /n/
​- The ‌spelling fafnir ​is a ‌normalized phonetic ​reconstruction; Younger ‌Futhark does ​not distinguish ‌voiced/voiceless stops ​or separate ‌short and ​long vowels

​The name ‌is Old ‌Norse *Fáfnir*, ‌written in ​the Latin ​alphabet by ‌the medieval ​Icelandic scribes ​of the ‌Codex Regius ​and Vǫlsunga ​saga. A ‌Viking-Age carver ​would have ‌rendered it ​in the ​Younger Futhark ​— a ​plausible runic ‌spelling is ‌ᚠᛅᚠᚾᛁᚱ — ​and the ‌sixteen-rune row ​of that ​period does ‌not mark ‌vowel length ‌at all: ‌the acute ​accent on ‌á is ​the modern ​editorial normalization ​that records ‌the long ​vowel which ​metre and ​grammar attest. ‌The Unicode ​restoration *Fáfnir* ​keeps that ​mark. As ‌a registrable ​domain the ‌restoration becomes ​fáfnir.com, which ‌IDNA encodes ​as the ‌punycode *xn--ffnir-xqa.com* ‌— the ​long á ​travelling intact ​through the ​machinery that ‌plain ASCII ‌would strip ​away.

domains.body:
In the ​norse tradition, **Fáfnir** ‌governed gold, ‌greed, and the ​metamorphosis that greed ​performs. The son ​of Hreiðmarr who ​became the ​dragon of Gnitaheiðr, ‌he is the ​living proof of ​the curse ‌he served: the ​weregild gold of ‌the dwarf Andvari ​unmade a ‌farmer's son into ​a poison-breathing serpent, ​and turned a ​name that means ​*the embracer* ​into an emblem ‌of everything that ​hoarding destroys.

His ‌domain is ​the moral underside ‌of heroic legend: ​patricide for an ‌inheritance, kinship dissolved ​by a ‌ring, and the ​slow alchemical change ​of a man ‌into the ‌monster that guards ‌what he cannot ​use. When Sigurðr's ​sword found ‌his heart, the ​gold passed on ​— and the ‌curse passed with ​it, through ​the hall of ‌the Gjúkungs to ​the ruin of ‌the whole ​Vǫlsung line.[^1]

### ​Andvaranautr

The ring ​of the dwarf ​Andvari, taken by ‌Loki as ‌ransom and cursed ​aloud to bring ‌death to every ​owner; it ​drove Fáfnir to ‌patricide.

### The ‌Worm of Gnitaheiðr

‌On the ‌Gnita heath greed ​finished its work: ‌Fáfnir took on ​the likeness of ​a serpent, ​lay upon his ‌father's gold, and ​breathed poison over ​the land.

​### Gramr

The ‌sword Reginn forged ​for his foster-son ​Sigurðr; from a ​trench dug ‌in the dragon's ​path, Sigurðr thrust ‌it upward into ​Fáfnir's heart.

‌### The Heart's ​Blood

Roasting the ‌dragon's heart, Sigurðr ‌burned his ​thumb and tasted ​the blood; at ​once he understood ​the speech of ‌birds and ‌heard the nuthatches ​betray Reginn.

sources.citation: Poetic Edda: Reginsmál, tr. Bellows (Internet Sacred Text Archive).

symbols.body:
The ​iconography associated ‌with ‌Fáfnir concentrates ​in ​a ​small set ​of ​recurring attributes, ‌each ​a compressed ​statement ‌about the ​name:[^1]

‌- **The ​hoard ‌of ​Andvari** — ​The ​weregild gold ​that ​ransomed Ótr's ‌skin ​and cursed ‌every ​hand it ‌passed ​through
‌- **Andvaranautr** ​— ‌The dwarf's ​ring, ​given up ‌last ‌and cursed ‌aloud: ​death to ​its ‌possessor ​and strife ​to ‌his house
​- ​**The serpent ‌shape** ​— The ‌ormr-form ​greed gave ​him ​on ​Gnitaheiðr; the ‌Eddas' ‌dragon crawls ​to ‌his water ​— ​the winged ‌firedrake ‌belongs to ‌later ‌art
​- **The ‌ægishjálmr** ​— The ​helm ​of terror ‌he ​wore over ​the ​gold, which ‌he ​boasted ​made him ​stronger ‌than all
​- ‌**The heart's ​blood** ‌— The ​draught ‌of wisdom ‌that ​taught ​Sigurðr the ​speech ​of birds ‌and ‌unmasked Reginn's ​treachery

sources.citation: Vǫlsunga saga, tr. Morris & Magnússon (Project Gutenberg #1152).

mythology.body:
**Fáfnir** is the dragon at ​the hinge of the Vǫlsung cycle — born ‌the son of the farmer-mage Hreiðmarr, brother to ‌the shape-shifting Ótr and to Reginn the smith. ​When the gods paid the weregild for Ótr's ​death with the dwarf Andvari's cursed hoard, Fáfnir ​murdered his own father for the gold, refused ​Reginn his share, and withdrew to Gnitaheiðr, where ​greed slowly remade him: the Eddic poems call him ‌an *ormr*, a creeping serpent who lay upon ​his inheritance and breathed poison over the heath. ​His death at the hand of Reginn's foster-son ‌Sigurðr — struck from a trench beneath the ​dragon's path — is the pivot on which ‌the whole heroic tragedy turns, for the curse ​of the ring Andvaranautr passed on with the ‌gold to destroy every house that held it. The ​tale was carved in stone in eleventh-century Sweden, ​sung in the Codex Regius, and retold by ​Wagner and Tolkien; no Germanic legend has carried ​further.[^1]

### The Weregild of Ótr (Skáldskaparmál)

Óðinn, ​Hœnir, and Loki came traveling to a waterfall ‌where an otter sat eating a salmon, half-asleep. ​Loki killed the otter with a stone, and ‌the gods flayed it and carried the skin as ​a trophy — but the otter was *Ótr*, ‌son of Hreiðmarr, who had the craft to ​take that shape. That night Hreiðmarr seized the ‌gods and named the ransom: the otter-skin was ​to be filled with gold and covered with ‌gold, inside and out.

Loki borrowed Rán's net ​and caught the dwarf *Andvari*, who lived in ​the falls in the likeness of a pike, and ‌stripped him of his hoard down to the ‌last ring — *Andvaranautr*. Andvari cursed it as ‌he went into the rock: the gold would ​be the death of two brothers and the ​strife of eight princes, and no man should ‌joy in his wealth. When the skin was ​covered, Hreiðmarr saw one whisker still showing, and ​Óðinn had to give up the ring to hide ‌it. So the ransom that was meant to ​settle a killing carried a spoken curse into ​the house that received it.[^2]

### The Patricide ‌of Gnitaheiðr (Reginsmál)

Fáfnir and Reginn demanded the ​blood-gold from their father as their share after ‌Ótr. Hreiðmarr refused — and Fáfnir put his ​sword through his father *sofanda*, sleeping, while the ​old man called on his daughters to witness that ​his life was spent. Fáfnir took all the ​gold, and when Reginn asked for his inheritance, ‌Fáfnir gave him a plain no.

Then Fáfnir ‌went out to *Gnitaheiðr*, the Gnita heath, and ​there his greed finished what the curse had ‌begun: he took on the likeness of a ​serpent — *var í orms líki*, as Reginsmál ​puts it — and lay brooding on the gold, ‌wearing the *ægishjálmr*, the helm of terror that ‌all living things feared, and blowing poison across ‌the land so that none dared come near. ‌Reginn, the cunning smith, went to the court ​of King Hjálprekr and became foster-father to the ‌young Sigurðr, son of Sigmundr — and began, ​patiently, to point the boy at his brother.

​### The Strike from Beneath (Fáfnismál)

Reginn forged for ​Sigurðr the sword *Gramr*, so keen it sheared ‌a lock of wool drifting down the Rhine ​and split Reginn's anvil in two. On the ​heath Sigurðr dug a deep trench in the ​dragon's track to the water and lay down ‌in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead, blowing venom, ​Sigurðr thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The ​dying dragon questioned his killer — *Fáfnismál* grants him ​a long, sardonic deathbed dialogue — and warned ‌him twice: *þér verða þeir baugar at bana*, ​these rings will be your death.

Reginn cut ‌out the heart and set Sigurðr to roast ​it. Testing whether it was done, Sigurðr burned ‌his thumb and thrust it into his mouth ​— and the moment the dragon's heart-blood touched ‌his tongue, he understood the speech of birds. The ‌nuthatches in the thicket told him Reginn meant ​to betray him and claim the gold alone; ​Sigurðr struck off Reginn's head, ate the heart, ​and loaded the hoard onto his horse Grani. ​He had won the treasure — and inherited ‌the curse, which would ride with the gold ‌to the hall of the Gjúkungs and bring ​down the whole Vǫlsung line.

Poetic Edda: Fáfnismál, tr. Bellows (Internet Sacred Text Archive).

syncretism.body:
Fáfnir belongs ​to the ‌common Germanic ‌heroic stock rather ​than to ​any cult, and ​his closest ​kin are ​literary. The continental ‌redaction of ​the same legend-complex ​survives in ‌the Middle ​High German *Nibelungenlied*, ‌where Siegfried ​slays a ‌dragon and wins ​the hoard ​of the Nibelungs ​— though ​there the ​dragon and the ‌curse have ​drifted apart, the ‌hoard's doom ​attaching to ‌the Burgundian kings ​instead. The ‌Old English *Beowulf* ​offers the ‌nearest analogue ​scene: a fire-dragon ​coiled for ‌three hundred ‌years on a ‌barrow-hoard, roused ​by the theft ​of a ‌single cup, ​slain by a ​hero it ‌kills in turn. ​Comparison is ​often drawn ‌with the Indo-European ​serpent-slaying myth ‌— the ​storm-god's combat with ​a watery ​serpent — but ​Fáfnir is ‌a different ‌creature: not a ​chaos-monster opposed ‌to cosmic order ​but a ​man whom ‌avarice deformed, a ‌moral dragon ‌rather than ‌a cosmic one. ​The Norse ‌*Þiðrekssaga* preserves yet ​another redaction ​of the ​Reginn–Sigurðr material, and ‌in later ​Scandinavian folk tradition ​the dragon ​on the ‌gold-barrow became a ​standing figure ​of sterile, hoarded ​wealth. The ‌line descends ​unbroken into modern ‌fantasy: Tolkien's ​Smaug is ‌openly the heir ​of Fáfnismál's ‌talking, riddle-loving worm.[^1]

‌Within the ​Norse tradition, ​closely related names ​in the ​corpus include [[alfheimr|Álfheimr]], ‌[[bifrost|Bifrǫst]], [[buri|Búri]], ‌[[eggther|Eggþér]], [[helheimr|Helheimr]], ​and [[hermod|Hermóðr]].

sources.citation: Vǫlsunga saga, tr. Morris & Magnússon (Project Gutenberg #1152).

cultural-legacy.body: Wagner fixed ​the dragon's ‌modern image: ‌in *Siegfried*, the ​third opera ​of the ​*Ring des Nibelungen*, ​the giant ​Fafner — ‌who has already ​murdered his ​brother Fasolt ‌for the ring ​— has ‌used the ​Tarnhelm to become ‌a dragon ​and sleeps ​on the hoard ​in a ​forest cave ​until Siegfried's sword ‌Nothung finds ​his heart; tasting ‌the blood, ​Wagner's Siegfried ‌likewise comes to ​understand the ‌Woodbird and, ​warned by it, ‌kills the ​treacherous Mime. ​Wagner conflated Hreiðmarr's ‌sons with ‌the giant ‌brothers of his ​own invention, ​but the ‌kinslaying for gold ​and the ​blood-taught birdsong ‌come straight from ​Reginsmál and ​Fáfnismál. Tolkien ‌acknowledged Fáfnir among ​the chief ‌models for ​Smaug — the ​speaking dragon ​on his ​gold, with the ‌one unarmoured ‌patch beneath. ​In comics, Marvel's ‌Fafnir appears ​as a ​Thor antagonist, the ‌monstrous king ‌of Nastrond; ‌in games the ‌name surfaces ​from *Final ‌Fantasy* to *Smite* ​and *God ​of War*, ​where Fáfnir is ‌remembered as ​a dwarf whose ​greed turned ​him dragon. ‌The idiom of ​the dragon-hoard ​— wealth ​kept and never ‌used — ​is his ‌permanent bequest to ​the language ‌of moralists. ​In modern Heathenry ‌Fáfnir is ‌no object ​of cult but ​a cautionary ​emblem: the ​man who embraced ‌gold until ‌the embrace ​became scales.[^1]

sources.citation: Vǫlsunga saga, tr. Morris & Magnússon (Project Gutenberg #1152).

archaeology.body: The ​Fáfnir story ‌is the ‌most frequently ​illustrated narrative ​of ​the late ​Viking Age. ​The Ramsund ‌carving (Sö ​101) ​and the ‌Gök stone ​(Sö 327), ‌both eleventh-century ​monuments ‌in Södermanland, ​Sweden, depict ​the whole ​cycle: Sigurðr ​thrusting ​his sword ‌up through ​the serpent's ‌body ​from below, ‌the horse ​Grani, Reginn ‌slain beside ​his ‌smith's tools, ​the birds ​in the ‌tree, and ‌Sigurðr ‌sucking his ​burned thumb ​over the ‌roasting fire. ​The ​carved portal ‌of Hylestad ​stave church ​in Norway ‌(c. ​1200, now ‌in the ​University Museum ​of Bergen) ​shows ​Reginn forging ‌the sword ‌and the ​dragon's death, ‌and ​crosses from ​the Isle ‌of Man ‌— Jurby ‌and ‌Kirk Andreas ​among them ‌— carry ​the same ​Sigurðr ​iconography into ‌the Irish ​Sea world. ​On ​the textual ‌side, Reginsmál ​and Fáfnismál ​survive in ​the ‌Codex Regius ​of the ‌Poetic Edda ​(GKS 2365 ‌4to, ​c. 1270), ‌and Vǫlsunga ‌saga is ​preserved most ​fully ​in the ​vellum NKS ‌1824 b ‌4to (c. ​1400).[^1]

poetic-edda.body: Fáfnir's ​Eddic ‌life ‌fills ​two heroic ​lays ​of ​the ​Codex ‌Regius. ​*Reginsmál* ​tells ‌the weregild ​of ‌Ótr: ​[[loki|Loki]] ‌kills ​the ​otter, ​Hreiðmarr ​names the ​ransom, ‌and ​the ‌dwarf ​[[andvari|Andvari]], ‌stripped ​of ‌his hoard ​in ‌Rán's ​net, ​lays ‌the ‌curse ‌on ​the ring ​Andvaranautr ‌— ​'the ​death ‌of ​two ​brothers ‌and the ​strife ‌of ​eight ​princes'.[^1] ​*Fáfnismál* ​stages ‌the ‌end at ​Gnitaheiðr: ‌[[sigurd|Sigurðr]], ​dug ​into ‌a ‌trench ‌beneath ‌the dragon's ​path, ‌thrusts ​Gramr ​upward, ​and ‌the ​dying ​Fáfnir trades ​warnings ‌and ​wisdom ​with ​his ‌slayer ​before ‌[[reginn|Reginn]]'s own ​treachery ‌is ​repaid.[^2] ‌*Grípisspá* ‌foretells ​the ​whole ​arc before ​a ‌sword ‌is ​drawn.[^3]
